messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Avoid People: avoid other people, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The event that fractured Mateo’s world happened in the parking lot of a grocery store, two years ago. He was thirty-eight then, a graphic designer in the suburbs of Chicago, married to a woman he adored, and he had never had a problem with police. That evening, he had stopped for milk. A patrol car pulled into the lot, lights off, no siren. Two officers got out and began shouting at a teenager on the sidewalk. Mateo, walking toward his car, was caught in the periphery. He froze. One officer turned, saw him, and in the space of a breath, Mateo was on the ground, his face pressed into the asphalt, a knee in his back, a voice screaming at him to stay down. He was held for fifteen minutes. They released him without charge. The officer who had knelt on him said nothing. Mateo drove home with the taste of gravel in his mouth and a bruise that bloomed across his ribs for a week.

In the months that followed, Mateo began to change. He could not explain what had happened when his wife asked; the words would tangle, his throat would close, and he would have to leave the room. What frightened him most was how the memory returned without warning. A car door slamming in a commercial could bring the full scene back, the weight on his back, the shouting, the smell of hot asphalt, and he would be so overwhelmed by emotion that he had to stop whatever he was doing. He began to avoid people, because being around anyone—especially strangers—made him feel too exposed. He told himself he was just tired. But the world felt hollow. Nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore, and he was certain that his life had been destroyed by what happened, that the injustice of it had been ignored and nothing had been done to fix it. He could not relax, even at home. His body stayed tense, always ready, and before he could feel comfortable anywhere, he would scan for exits, running through escape routes in his head.

He coped by keeping his mind occupied all the time. He spent long hours on his phone, scrolling through design feeds, playing puzzle games, clicking through articles he did not finish. The moment he stopped, the memory would surface again, and the surge of helplessness would return. So he did not stop. He worked late into the night at his desk, sketching logos he would never send, because the quiet of the house was worse. The screen became his refuge, but it also kept the memory alive: every time he put the phone down, the memory hit harder, as if it had been waiting. He began to notice that even the sight of visible injuries or wounds on others—a bandage on a coworker’s hand, a child’s scraped knee—could trigger the full memory, the same rush of heat and dread. And the presence of police, even a patrol car passing on the highway, would make his heart pound and his mind go blank, and then the memory would come, and he would be back on the ground.

Mateo’s wife, Sarah, began to notice that he was never present. He would sit beside her on the couch, phone in hand, eyes fixed on a screen, his shoulders tight. She tried to talk to him. He said he was fine. But he was not fine. He could not relax, and the more he could not relax, the more he scanned for threats, and the more he scanned, the more the memory returned, unbidden, overwhelming. The memory itself made his body go on alert, and the alertness made the memory more vivid. He began to believe that the world was dangerous, that he had been singled out, that no one would listen. The injustice of it gnawed at him, and that sense of being wronged made him feel even more unsafe, as if the same thing could happen again at any moment. He started to see police where there were none, to flinch at the sound of a car door, to feel the asphalt under his cheek in the middle of a work meeting.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment three weeks ago. He was at the grocery store again, the same chain, different parking lot. A man in a dark jacket walked past him. Mateo’s vision narrowed. He dropped his basket, walked out, and sat in his car for forty minutes, shaking, unable to drive. That night, Sarah told him she could not live like this anymore. She was not leaving, she said, but she needed him to try. He is afraid that trying will mean talking about what happened, and he is not sure he can finish the story out loud. But he is more afraid of losing her, and of the life he once had. So he came.
